prompt:
An athlete monitors daily fluid intake and body hydration during intensive training.
(a) The athlete drinks roughly 8 glasses of water each day. Each glass has an estimated volume of $250\text{ cm}^3$.
(i) Calculate the total estimated volume of water consumed per day in $\text{cm}^3$. [1]
(ii) Convert this volume into litres, where $1\text{ litre} = 1000\text{ cm}^3$. [1]
(b) Given that water has a density of $1.0\text{ kg per litre}$, state the estimated mass of this daily water intake in kilograms. [1]
(c) The athlete has an estimated body mass of $70\text{ kg}$.
(i) Calculate the daily water intake as an approximate percentage of the athlete's body mass. [2]
(ii) Explain why recording this daily water intake in a training journal as '$2000.00\text{ g}$' would be scientifically inappropriate. [1]

parts.description: State mass of water in kg

part_enrichment.guidance: Award M1 for (2.0 / 70) x 100%, and A1 for 2.9% (accept 2.8% to 3.0%).
Award B1 for explaining that stating two decimal places in grams implies precision to 0.01 g which an estimate of 'about 8 glasses' cannot justify.

answer:
(a)(i) 2000 cm^3
(a)(ii) 2.0 litres
(b) 2.0 kg
(c)(i) 2.9% (accept 2.8% to 3.0%)
(c)(ii) Stating '2000.00 g' claims false precision to 0.01 g that a rough estimate of 'about 8 glasses' cannot support.

mark_scheme.criterion: (c)(ii) Explains that the trailing zeroes imply false measurement precision (to 0.01 g) that is completely unsupported by visual estimation of glassfuls.

hints: Multiply number of glasses by volume per glass.
Use 1000 cm^3 = 1 litre, and 1 litre of water = 1 kg.
Divide water mass by athlete mass for percentage.
Why are extra zeroes misleading when counting rough glassfuls?
solution:
(a)(i) Total volume = 8 x 250 cm^3 = 2000 cm^3.
(a)(ii) Volume in litres = (2000 cm^3) / 1000 = 2.0 litres.
(b) Mass = density x volume = (1.0 kg/L) x 2.0 L = 2.0 kg.
(c)(i) Percentage of body mass = (2.0 kg / 70 kg) x 100% = 2.86% approx 2.9% (or ~3%).
(c)(ii) Writing '2000.00 g' specifies six significant figures, claiming that the fluid intake is measured down to the nearest 0.01 g (hundredth of a gram). An estimate based on counting rough glassfuls has an uncertainty of tens or hundreds of grams. Reporting six digits is scientifically dishonest false precision.
teacher_walkthrough: Integrates volume estimation, liquid density conversion, percentage scaling, and precision ethics.
Review each marking point to demonstrate how marks accumulate across applied estimation tasks.
